## SUMMARY

The complexity of regeneration extends beyond local wound responses, eliciting systemic processes across the entire organism. However, the functional relevance and coordination of distant molecular processes remain unclear. In the cnidarian Nematostella vectensis, we show that local regeneration triggers a systemic homeostatic response, leading to coordinated whole-body remodeling. Leveraging spatial transcriptomics, endogenous protein tagging, and live imaging, we comprehensively dissect this systemic response at the organismal scale. We identify proteolysis as a critical process driven by both local and systemic upregulation of metalloproteases. We show that metalloproteinase expression levels and activity scale with the extent of tissue loss. This proportional response drives long-range tissue and extracellular matrix movement. Our ﬁndings demonstrate the adaptive nature of the systematic response in regeneration, enabling the organism to maintain shape homeostasis while coping with a wide range of injuries.

## INTRODUCTION

The regenerative capacity in the animal kingdom is remarkably diverse,1,2 encompassing extensive whole-body regeneration in invertebrates such as cnidarians and planarians, in stark contrast to the more restricted, tissue-speciﬁc regeneration in vertebrates3–5 (Figure 1A). This array of regenerative phenomena reﬂects a broad spectrum of biological resilience across animal lineages. Despite this diversity, a common thread is the initiation of both localized and systemic responses to tissue injury, manifested through a series of cellular and molecular events.6–10

In regenerative models such as the axolotl, limb amputation triggers cell-cycle reactivation not only at the wound site but also in distant organs, including the contralateral limb, spinal cord, liver, and heart.9 Analogous phenomena are observed in mice, where injury activates quiescent stem cells in remote tissues,8 and in zebraﬁsh, where cardiac injury induces gene expression changes in distant organs like the brain.7 Invertebrates also display similar patterns, with planarians and acoels

showing initial body-wide cellular proliferation post injury that becomes concentrated at the regeneration site.6,11 Moreover, interfering with long-range signaling can affect regenerative outcomes, as observed in planarians.12 Such insights highlight the need for a holistic approach to understanding the complex processes underlying regeneration across different animal taxa. Our study focuses on the starlet sea anemone, Nematostella vectensis, a cnidarian known for its extensive whole-body regeneration capabilities.13,14 We leverage its genetic tractability15,16 to conduct an in-depth investigation of regeneration, comparing intact and regenerating animals, from genomewide expression patterns and molecular activities to tissue dynamics and overall organismal shape. The relatively simple morphology yet complex tissue architecture of the Nematostella polyp, with its bi-layered tissue and interstitial mesoglea (also known as extracellular matrix [ECM]), supports a diverse range of cell types along its body axis.17,18 Key cellular mechanisms, particularly proliferation and apoptosis, play critical roles in oral regeneration.13,14,19

## RESULTS

Spatial transcriptomics of intact polyps To characterize spatial gene expression patterns in intact animals, we employed RNA tomography (tomo-seq) on unfed, primary polyps (approximately 1 mm in length) along the oral-aboral axis (Figures 1B and S1A). Brieﬂy, this technique combines tissue cryosectioning with RNA sequencing on individual sections to generate an expression atlas with uni-dimensional spatial information.20–22 We processed six polyps at a resolution of 20-mm slices, yielding a total of 331 slices (Figures 1B and S1A; Table S1; following quality control, yielding 50–60 slices per polyp). To accommodate variations in animal length and resulting slice numbers, we considered two complementary strategies foraligning the spatial transcriptomic data across polyps (Figure S1B). We ﬁrst aligned slices from all polyps to a common coordinate system using reference-based alignment with dynamic time warping23 (Figure S1B). To achieve this, we selected a high-quality reference polyp (Figure S1A; method details) and identiﬁed its 500 most highly variable genes (HVGs), which displayed distinct expression patterns across the polyp (Figure S1C; Table S2). This alignment revealed consistent spatial expression patterns along the oral-aboral axis (Figures S1D and S1E). Second, to mitigate potential bias from a single reference, we employed Harmony24 for integrated analysis of transcriptomes from all polyp slices (Figures S1B and S1F). Unbiased clustering (Louvain, resolution 0.8) on aligned Harmony components identiﬁed ﬁve distinct gene expression states, yielding 1,276 clusterspeciﬁc marker genes (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, log2fold change [FC] > 0.3) (Figure S1F; Table S2). To visualize the high-dimensional tomo-seq data, we constructed a two-dimensional single-cell projection and interactive graphing (SPRING) embedding for all slices (Figure 1C).25 This embedding visually resembled the polyp’s morphology. By grouping (binning) slice numbers and visualizing them on the SPRING plot (Figure 1D), a clear pattern emerged: lower slice numbers clustered at one end of the embedding, whereas higher numbers gathered at the opposite end, reﬂecting their spatial arrangement along the aboral-oral axis. We then used a diffusion map approach26 to estimate transcriptome-based pseudo-locations for each slice, creating a uniﬁed slice index system, as the original indexes varied across polyps (Figures 1D and S1A). Remarkably, the pseudo-ordering largely mirrored the original slice ordering within each polyp (Figures S1G and S1H), with minor discrepancies observed mainly in lower-quality slices (Figure S1I). The embedding also recapitulated known oral-aboral gene expression patterns, such as cadherin 1/3,27 Otx,28 repulsive guidance molecule (RGM),29 and nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRc)30 (Figure 1C). Focusing on the top markers for each cluster, this combined alignment and embedding approach consolidated the set of regional markers to 583 spatially variable genes (Figures 1E and S1J; Table S2). To validate some of the identiﬁed regional markers, we performed an in situ hybridization chain reaction (HCR) for several

genes with distinct spatial expression patterns (Figures 1E, 1F, and S1K). We compiled a list that combined annotated and unannotated genes. Of the 16 genes tested, 15 largely exhibited the expected expression patterns, with the exception of HSPA12A, which showed no detectable signal. Interestingly, in situ HCR revealed cell-type-speciﬁc expression for some genes, a detail not discernible from the slice resolution of the tomo-seq data. Speciﬁcally, we identiﬁed four unannotated genes (unknown-003672, unknown-011036, unknown-003854, and unknown-015111) exhibiting mesentery-speciﬁc expression. In conclusion, these ﬁndings demonstrate that the spatially aligned transcriptomic maps effectively identify robust gene expression domains along the oral-aboral axis of primary polyps.

Spatiotemporal transcriptomics of regenerating polyps Leveraging spatial transcriptomic maps created for intact animals, we sought to determine the degree to which the amputation of one extremity of the poly can induce dynamic changes in gene expression throughout the entire body. We choose the physa (aboral end) for removal due to its morphological simplicity and convenience compared with the complex oral structures, as well as the availability of the Fgfrb-EGFP transgenic line marking the aboral pole tip.31 Approximately 20% of the polyp was amputated, followed by transcriptomic analysis and tracking the reestablishment of Fgfrb-EGFP expressing cells as a proxy for regeneration (Figure 2A). Quantiﬁcation of the intensity proﬁles showed that aboral Fgfrb-EGFP expression reappeared around 24 h post amputation (hpa) and was fully restored at 48 hpa (Figure 2A). To capture the complete regeneration dynamics, we collected and analyzed slices from three to four polyps per time point at 12, 24, 48, and 96 hpa (Figure S2A; Table S1, following quality control, yielding 36–56 slices per polyp). To investigate both local and global effects of surgical physa removal, we integrated the tomo-seq slices from intact and regenerating animals using the reference-free Harmony approach (Figures 2B, S2B, and S2C). This method was favored for its comprehensive and unbiased integration of tomo-seq data across all analyzed animals (Figure S1B), followed by clustering and pseudo-time inference, resulting in a dataset with 957 integrated slices. Consistent with ﬁndings from intact animals, the aboral-oral axis was identiﬁed as the primary source of gene expression variation among tomo-seq slices in regenerating animals (Figures 2B and S2C). The joint embedding generated a coherent coordinate system across intact and amputated animals (Figures 2B and S2D–S2G), enabling visualization of gene expression across all slices and time points. The persistence of axial marker expression in regenerating polyps further conﬁrmed that the aboral-oral axis is the major source of gene expression variation in regenerating polyps (Figures 2C and S2H–S2J). Thus, we generated robust spatiotemporal molecular maps for regenerating animals, demonstrating a close resemblance to the spatiotemporal gene expression proﬁles of intact polyps.

Dual orchestration of morphallactic and epimorphic processes As the onset of cell proliferation often demarcates the transition from wound healing to regeneration, we initially assessed spatial expression patterns of known cell-cycle genes (MKI67, CDK1, AURKA, TACC3, and CENPA) between 12 and 96 hpa (Figures 2D and S3A–S3C). Dynamic expression was observed in regenerating tissue, with consistent upregulation at 24 hpa and a return to near-basal levels by 96 hpa (Figure 2D). Intriguingly, these genes were gradually upregulated toward the oral pole, suggesting a distal response to tissue damage even though the oral tissue was not damaged (Figures 2D and S3B). To conﬁrm this proliferation pattern, we employed EdU labeling to mark cells in the S-phase along the oral-aboral axis from 5 to 96 hpa (Figures 2E and S3D). A moderate, transient increase in EdU+ cells was observed at the wound site between 16 and 48 hpa (Figures 2E and S3E), contrasting the massive proliferation seen during oral regeneration,13,14 suggesting distinct cellular mechanisms.32 Additionally, there was a marked increase in EdU+ cells toward the oral pole, peaking at 16– 24 hpa and decreasing by 40 hpa. Although this pattern differs from the proliferation typically seen during oral regeneration,13,14

it supports our spatial transcriptomics, reinforcing the notion of proliferation being stimulated in regions distant from the immediate site of regeneration. Motivated by the observation in the cnidarian Hydractinia that remote proliferative cells migrate toward the regenerating tissue,33 we performed a photoconversion experiment to monitor the movement of photoconverted Kaede-positive cells at the oral pole following amputation (Figures 2F and S3F). No discernible movement of photoconverted oral cells was observed toward the regenerating physa (Figure 2F), indicating that the oral tissue does not directly contribute to physa regeneration. However, analysis of photoconverted tissues revealed notable changes in patch shape and position (Figure 2F). In physa-amputated animals, patches near the oral pole occasionally shifted toward the tentacles, whereas those in intact animals remained largely stationary. The most striking effect was the elongation of photoconverted patches along the main body axis following physa amputation. To assess the extent of this phenomenon, we extended the photoconversion experiment to the body column (Figures 3A, S4A, and S4B). Quantiﬁcation of patch shape (aspect ratios) and displacement revealed that, unlike intact polyps, physa-amputated polyps exhibited patch elongation and displacement (Figures 3A, 3B, and S4B), transforming from squares to rectangles. This axial shape change suggested body-wide, oriented cell rearrangement, subsequently increasing inter-patch spacing. We hypothesized that this morphallactic remodeling represents a global readjustment of polyp shape, potentially reﬂected in changes in aspect ratio (polyp length/average width). To test this, we performed physa and mid-body amputations, measuring changes in polyp dimensions during regeneration (Figures 3C, 3D, and S4C). Both amputations led to increased body length and decreased body width, with more pronounced changes in mid-body amputations. Although physa-amputated polyps fully restored the aspect ratio of intact polyps by day 8, mid-body-amputated polyps approached but did not fully reach this ratio (Figures 3C, 3D, and S4D). These ﬁndings reveal a complex systemic regenerative

mechanism involving wound-localized and distal cell proliferation coupled with morphallactic remodeling. This process appears to dynamically adjust homeostatic balance, achieving a ‘‘preferred’’ polyp shape by altering the relationship between polyp length and width during regeneration.

Molecular landscape of systemic homeostatic response Having established the dual deployment of morphallactic and epimorphic processes during physa regeneration, we next set out to identify molecular processes that change in response to amputation (Figure 4A). We conducted a global body-wide differential expression analysis, separately considering an early regenerative stage (12/24 hpa), a mid-regenerative stage (24/ 48 hpa), and a late stage (48/96 hpa). To identify stage-speciﬁc molecular processes, we then tested for positively differentially expressed (DE) genes at each stage versus all other time points as well as the intact animal (early: N = 215, mid: N = 216, late: N = 189,Wilcoxon rank-sum test, log2FC > 0.5; Table S3). Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis (top 50 genes per stage; GOseq p value < 0.05; Figures 4C and S4E; Table S3) identiﬁed distinct molecular processes that mark these three regeneration stages (Figures 4B and 4C). The early phase of regeneration was marked by an increase in proteolytic genes, including metallopeptidase ADAMTS6 and BP10 (Figures 4B and 4D). This observation is consistent with previous transcriptomic studies on wound or regenerating polyps,10,35 highlighting their potential role in remodeling the ECM and processing growth factors. Transitioning to the mid-regenerative phase, a second set of genes became prominent, notably involved in cell communication, exempliﬁed by Fras1 and Frem2. These genes are recognized for their contributions to basement membrane integrity in other systems.36,37 Finally, the late regeneration was characterized by an upregulation of G-protein-coupled receptors, including gamma-aminobutyric acid B receptor 2 (GABBR2) and adhesion G-protein-coupled receptor V1 (ADGRV1). The sequential activation of distinct molecular events across regeneration stages demonstrates a coordinated molecular cascade of the systemic response in regeneration. We further assessed whether gene expression changes in response to the injury also occurred in more localized patterns across the body. To investigate the spatial dynamics of gene expression during regeneration, we adapted a Gaussian process model38 to test for positionally local differential expressed genes (spatial DE genes) between each regeneration time point and the intact reference (Figure 4E). Across all time points, this analysis identiﬁed 702 spatial DE genes (false discovery rate [FDR] < 1%) (Figure S4F). Remarkably, 35% of these genes had evidence for differential spatial expression across all regeneration stages (Figure S4F). GO enrichment analysis34 identiﬁed proteolysis (p value < 0.02; Figures 4F and S4G), which is in common with the global response process. Additionally, the analysis highlighted protein folding and iron homeostasis, which were exclusively identiﬁed by the local differential expression analysis. Within these categories, diverse patterns of spatial DE were identiﬁed (Figure S4G). For example, the carboxypeptidases CAP2 and CPA4 were DE away from the wound site, whereas the matrix metalloproteinase 17 (Mmp17) was spatially DE at the wound site and not expressed elsewhere. Beyond the recognized stress response role of heat shock genes in regeneration,39–42 their additional expression patterns hint at a broader physiological signiﬁcance in polyp biology. These ﬁndings underscore a complex molecular landscape of the systemic response in regeneration, shifting the organism from a steady to a dynamic state, with proteolysis involved in diverse spatial response patterns.

Local and systemic regulation of metalloproteases Upregulation of proteolysis genes, as identiﬁed in both the global and local analysis of the gene expression response to injury, led us to hypothesize a widespread activation of metalloproteases across the organism. To test this hypothesis, we employed in vivo zymography,43 a method that allows for the spatial visualization of proteolytic activity through the cleavage of a dye-quenched (DQ-) substrate, resulting in ﬂuorescence (Figures 5A, 5B, and S5A). At 15 h post incubation with the DQ-Col4, intact polyps ex-

hibited a basal level of ﬂuorescence signal indicative of normal homeostatic metalloprotease activities. In contrast, polyps subjected to physa amputation demonstrated a widespread and intense ﬂuorescence signal distribution, suggesting a systemic induction of hydrolytic enzyme activities in regeneration, despite the localized nature of the injury. Intriguingly, this upregulation was even more enhanced in response to an increase in tissue loss following mid-body amputation (Figures 5A, 5B, and S5A), reﬂecting the extensive tissue remodeling demands following more severe damage. To link the changes in proteolytic activity levels to the identiﬁed gene expression response, we analyzed the expression patterns of both genes with local response at the wound site as well as systematic body-responding metalloenzymes using HCR (Figure 5C). Consistent with the tomo-seq data, the expression of Mmp17 and its associated matrix metalloprotease inhibitor 3 (Mmpi3) was activated locally at the wound site, whereas ADAMTS6 was ubiquitously upregulated in response to physa amputation (Figures 5C, 5D, and S5B–S5D). By 18 hpa, a signiﬁcant global displacement of the Col4::Dendra2 patches was evident in physa-amputated animals (Figure 6C), contrasting with the minimal displacement observed in intact polyps. Notably, the regenerating animals exhibited bidirectional movement of the patches, with those near the mouth movingorally and those lower down moving aborally, concomitant witha decreasein patch intensity (Figure 6C). This globalalteration in ECM dynamics mirrored distal epithelial rearrangements observed previously (Figures 2F and S3F), suggesting a coordinated displacement of epithelial cells and ECM as a composite structure during physa regeneration. To test the dependency of this systemic basement membrane remodeling on metalloprotease activity, we repeated the Col4::Dendra2 photoconversion experiment in physa-regenerating animals, with and without the matrix metalloprotease inhibitor GM6001. We found that GM6001 treatment effectively prevented the displacement of photoconverted patches typically seen in physa-regenerating animals (Figures6Dand6E).Furthermore,inhibitingmetalloproteaseactivity resulted in a disruption of polyp shape (Figure 6E), indicating that the systemic activation of metalloproteases is a driving force behind global basement membrane remodeling, thereby facilitating the reshaping of the polyp during regeneration. To further examine the effect of the matrix metalloprotease inhibition on the local regenerative response, both physa-amputated and orally amputated Fgfrb-EGFP polyps were treated with GM6001. Although wound closure and restoration of epithelial integrity occurred in both scenarios (Figures 6F–6I, S6C, and S6D), Fgfrb-EGFP expression in GM6001-treated physa-amputated polyps was only partially restored compared with controls (Figure 6G). Moreover, oral regeneration in GM6001-treated polyps predominantly arrested upon wound closure (Figures 6H and 6I), with few progressing to the early bud stage. Taken together, these results demonstrate the critical role of matrix metalloproteases, both locally and systemically, and underscore their profound impact on the morphogenetic processes that are essential for successful regeneration.

## DISCUSSION

The ﬁeld of regeneration has traditionally focused on woundlocalized processes. Here, we provide a mechanistic under-

standing of how regeneration extends far beyond the wound site, involving a cascade of systemic processes that orchestrate coordinated whole-body remodeling. To elucidate these intricate mechanisms, we combined spatial transcriptomics, endogenous protein tagging, and live imaging, comparing intact and physa-regenerating polyps. These data serve as invaluable resources to gain deeper insights into the inherent biology of a highly regenerative species and demonstrate the complex mechanisms underpinning regeneration. A central ﬁnding of our study highlights the signiﬁcant role of proteolysis, driven by systemic upregulation of metalloproteinases, in achieving shape homeostasis during regeneration. Shape homeostasis refers to the organism’s ability to restore and maintain its characteristic proportions following structural perturbations such as tissue loss, thereby potentially ensuring functional integrity. The expression levels and activity of these enzymes scale with the extent of tissue loss, enabling an adaptive, coordinated remodeling of the whole animal in regeneration. This proportionate effect was also reﬂected in the extent of bidirectional ﬂow of both epithelial cells and their underlying ECM. This bidirectional pattern mirrors similar dynamics in Hydra, where continuous tissue and mesoglea movements are part of homeostasis.44,45 In Nematostella, however, such movement is triggered by injury, showing the dynamic nature of the cnidarian mesoglea. Previous work has identiﬁed localized ECM changes in the regeneration of other organisms,46–49 but our study brings attention to body-wide ECM changes governed by metalloproteases and leading to the gradual reshaping of the whole-body after tissue loss. Although we still do not know whether juvenile and adult polyps also deploy this mechanism, we propose that it is pivotal in facilitating extensive tissue remodeling and is likely a common strategy in species capable of whole-body regeneration. Our work also uncovered a surprising induction of local cell proliferation at the oral pole in response to physa amputation, despite these cells not contributing directly to the regenerating tissue. This distal proliferation could be part of a global stress response, possibly involving the production of defense cells such as stinging cells. This distal oral proliferation, coupled with the identiﬁcation of diverse spatiotemporal gene expression responses and the long-range tissue and ECM dynamics, suggests the existence of a complex, body-wide regulatory mechanism initiated by local tissue loss. In mice, a systemic protease activated by tissue injury relays a signal to stem cells in noninjured tissues to enter an activated state, enhancing their ability to repair damage.50 Post injury, long-distance communication can also be orchestrated by other factors, including Erk activity,12,51,52 the JAK/STAT pathway,53 and the engagement of the peripheral nervous system.54 However, the discovery of a scaled response in regeneration in our study indicates that the sea anemone Nematostella can interpret varying degrees of tissue loss and translate this into scaled gene expression, enabling investigation of the mechanisms of such adaptability. In summary, our ﬁndings reveal a complex interplay of local and systemic responses in regeneration, underscoring the need for comprehensive organism-level studies to fully understand the mechanisms of regenerative capabilities across species.

Limitations of the study Although our study presents robust molecular and cellular evidence supporting the role of local and systemic responses in Nematostella regeneration, there are certain limitations to consider. First, the upstream mechanisms that regulate the scaling of the regenerative response remain incompletely understood. Speciﬁcally, it is unclear how the organism interprets varying degrees of tissue loss and whether downstream effectors spatially sense the location of amputation. Furthermore, our study focuses exclusively on regeneration in primary polyps, leaving the applicability of shape homeostasis mechanisms in other life stages unexplored. Future studies are required to assess the functional relevance of shape homeostasis and determine whether these processes are conserved across regenerating juveniles and adults.

METHOD DETAILS

Tomography mRNA sequencing Relaxed polyps were immobilized with 7% MgCl2 in 12 ppt artiﬁcial seawater (ASW). Mounting and storage of the samples were done as previously described.65 Changes to the protocol are described below. Polyps were transferred via mouth pipette into the Tissue Freezing Medium (Leica) and oriented using a hair tool so that its tentacles were fully extended parallel to the body column. The ends of the animal were marked with red polyethylene microspheres (Cospheric, REDPMS-0.98 180-212 mm). Samples were frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at -80C. Samples were warmed to -20C prior to cryosectioning into 20-micron thick slices. Each slice was transferred into a separate well of a 96-well tomo-seq plate (Single Cell Discoveries, scdiscoveries.com). Processing of the plates and library preparation was then carried out by Single Cell Discoveries following a CEL-seq2 protocol66 adapted for a low-input robotics system. Libraries were then multiplexed and sequenced on the Illumina NextSeq500 platform using the 40 bp paired-end setup. A sequencing depth of 50-80 million reads was generated per library.

In situ hybridization chain reaction (HCR) Genes with high mean expression levels were selected, and their presence in the Nematostella genome was conﬁrmed through PCR ampliﬁcation of the genomic regions corresponding to each selected gene. For each gene target (Table S2), probe sets for in situ HCR v3.0 with split-initiator probes were ordered from Molecular Instruments, Inc (molecularinstruments.com). DNA HCR ampliﬁers, hybridization, wash, and ampliﬁcation buffers were also purchased from Molecular Instruments. The staining protocol used for in situ HCR was adapted from Molecular Instrument’s protocol for whole-mount zebraﬁsh embryos and larvae, based on Choi and colleagues.67 Brieﬂy, polyps were ﬁxed with 4% PFA in PTw (1x PBS, 0.1% tween-20) for 1 hour at room temperature. Samples were then permeabilized with 10% DMSO in PBS, followed by PTx0.5 (1x PBS, 0.5% Triton X-100). Tissue was then clariﬁed via MeOH washes (30%, 60%, 100%) and stored at -20C for >1 hour before rehydration back into PTw. Samples were then treated with 10 mg/ml Proteinase K (Promega V3021) in PTw for 30min. Excess Proteinase K was removed by washing with PTw. Animals were then reﬁxed in 4% PFA in PTw for 25 min and washed 3 times with PTw. Prehybridization was done in 200 mL Probe Hybridization Buffer (Molecular Instruments) for 30 min at 37C before hybridizing with the in situ probe set (2 pmol in 200 mL Probe hybridization Buffer) overnight at 37C. In the case of four-channel HCR, Proteinase K treatment and postﬁxation were omitted from the protocol. Post-hybridization washes are as follows: 2 times 30 min washes with 400 mL Probe Wash Buffer (Molecular Instruments) at 37C, then 2 times 5 min washes with 500 mL 5X SSCT (5x SSC pH 7, 0.1% Tween-20) at room temperature. Ampliﬁer hairpins h1 and h2 (18 pmol) were heated separately to 95C for 90 sec, then snap-cooled to room temperature before being added to 300 mL Probe Ampliﬁcation Buffer (Molecular Instruments). Samples were then incubated with this ampliﬁcation solution overnight at room temperature. Excess hairpins were removed by the following washes: 2 times 5 min, then 2 times 30 min with 500 mL 5X SSCT. DNA counterstaining was done by incubating samples overnight with Hoechst (1:1000) in PTw at 4C. Samples were then mounted into 85% glycerol or Vectashield Plus (Vector Laboratories) or Slowfade Glass (Thermoﬁsher) for imaging. Confocal stacks of whole polyps were acquired on a Leica TCS SP8 confocal microscope using a 40x 1.1NA water objective using the tile scan function, or on a Leica Stellaris 8 using a 20x 0.75NA multi-immersion objective with Type F immersion oil. The acquired z-stack images were processed using Fiji (https://imagej.net/software/ﬁji/).58 For quantifying the HCR signal intensity, a sum intensity projection was applied to each image. This method involves summing up the pixel intensities across all slices of the z-stack, providing a cumulative measure of the signal intensity throughout the volume of each polyp. Using the straight line tool, the main body axis of each polyp in the projected image was delineated with a line of 150 mm width. This line served as the basis for extracting the ﬂuorescence intensity proﬁle. The ’Plot Proﬁle’ function in Fiji was then used to generate a graph representing the HCR signal intensity along the normalized length of the polyp’s body axis.

Full details on the generation of this transgenic line have been reported previously.31 Fgfrb-EGFP embryos were grown at 23C by crossing homozygous males with wild-type female adults. Primary polyps were transferred to a plastic Petri dish containing 12 ppt artiﬁcial seawater (ASW) and immobilized using 7% MgCl₂. Physa amputation was performed using a sharp knife, after which the polyps were moved to a dish with fresh 12 ppt ASW to remove residual MgCl₂. The polyps were then maintained in small glass dishes (30 polyps in 20 mL of 12 ppt ASW) at 23C until ﬁxation and antibody staining. For the aboral end, a region of interest (ROI) with ﬁxed dimensions was applied to all samples to obtain a proﬁle plot of the GFP signal along the aboral end. The ‘area under the curve’ (AUC) of individual proﬁle plots was calculated and subsequently plotted for analysis.

Sample ﬁxation and immunohistochemistry Animals were ﬁxed and stained using a modiﬁed protocol adapted from Genikhovich and Technau.68 Brieﬂy, samples were ﬁxed in a solution of 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA; Electron Microscopy Sciences E15710) in Ptw (1x PBS, 0.1% tween-20) for 1 hour at room temperature before being permeabilized with 10% DMSO in PBS for 20 min followed by Ptx 0.5 (1X PBS, 0.5% TritonX-100) for 20 min. Then they were incubated in blocking buffer (5% normal goat serum, 1% BSA, 1% DMSO, 0.1% TritonX-100 in 1X PBS) for 1 hour at room temperature before incubating with the primary antibody (anti-EGFP 1:500, Torry Pines TP401) overnight at 4C. Samples were then washed 3 times with PTw before incubating with the secondary antibody (goat anti-rabbit alexa488, 1:500, Thermo Fisher A-11008) and DNA stain (Hoechst34580 1:1000 Sigma Aldrich 63493). Samples were then washed with PTw 3 times and mounted into 85% glycerol or Vectashield Plus for imaging.

EdU staining and quantiﬁcation Staining with EdU was done as described previously.31 Brieﬂy, animals were incubated with 50 mM EdU in 12 ppt (parts per thousand) ASW (artiﬁcial sea water; seasalt from Instant Ocean) for 30 minutes before immobilizing with 7% MgCl2 solution. Animals were then ﬁxed with 4% PFA in PTw for 1 hour at room temperature before being permeabilized with 10% DMSO in PBS for 20 min followed by Ptx 0.5 (1X PBS, 0.5% TritonX-100) for 20 min. Samples were then blocked for 15 min using 5% BSA (Sigma A2153-50G) in PBS. The Click-it reaction was then performed with alexa647-azide with the sample as speciﬁed in the Click-it EdU Cell Proliferation Kit for Imaging (Thermo Fisher C10340) for 30 min at room temperature. Excess labelling reagents were washed away with PTw for 5 min before mounting into 85% glycerol for imaging. EdU+ cells were quantiﬁed using FIJI. First a difference of gaussians was calculated for each sample by subtracting the gaussian blurred (sigma = 2) maximum projection image from the gaussian blurred (sigma = 4) maximum projection image. The ‘‘ﬁnd maxima’’ function was then used to detect individual EdU+ cells and determine their location (x, y coordinates) along the animal body. The 2D Coordinates were then collapsed into 1D by taking only the coordinates corresponding to the oral-aboral axis. The coordinates were then normalized to the size of the animal for each sample to generate a uniform coordinate axis. The numbers of EdU+ cells were then binned into 100 bins and plotted as a heat map using ggplot2.

Tomo-seq data processing Reads were mapped to the Nematostella vectensis transcriptome55 using the kallisto-BUStools method.59 Full gene sequences were used for mapping as it resulted in consistently higher mapping rates compared with spliced transcripts when using exon-intron boundaries available in the genome annotation. Barcode (8bp) and UMI (6bp) locations in the sequence of the ﬁrst read were speciﬁed accordingly for pseudoalignment. Barcodes were corrected to account for 1 substitution using the white list of barcodes. UMI were then counted for each gene to provide a count matrix for each sample.

Quality control & sample boundaries Tomo-seq data for each polyp includes gene counts for 96 slices, some of which do not contain the polyp due to different alignment of polyps for the cutting process and varying polyp sizes. In addition, differences in tissue quality and sequencing depth lead to varying numbers of transcript counts detected per slice (Table S1) which made a dynamic threshold selection for each polyp needed. Sample boundaries were thus deﬁned automatically using a dynamic threshold for each polyp deﬁned as a local minimum of the density function of the number of genes per slice. Slices with high background signals above this threshold were marked and consequently ﬁltered out manually (see Figure 1A). A summary statistic of the remaining slices is shown in Table S1.

Regional marker genes selection in the reference animal Transcript counts for the genes detected in at least three animals were normalized by total expression per slice and log-transformed. A single reference polyp was selected based on two criteria: (1) no slices within the sample boundary were discarded due to low gene counts and (2) it had the highest average transcript count per slice (278,358 UMIs/slice) among all intact polyps (Table S1). The top 500 highly variable genes (HVGs) as identiﬁed for the reference polyp were considered as regional markers (Polyp 3 - HH7T7BGXF- 42, see Figure S1C). HGVs were identiﬁed by using the FindVariableFeatures function with vst selection method as implemented in ‘Seurat’ v4.62

Reference-based polyp alignment using dynamic time warping Polyp alignment using dynamic time warping was conducted using the implementation in the DTW package v1.22.23 In particular, an open-ended alignment with an asymmetric step function was performed. Thus, we allowed for the alignment of multiple slices within the query polyp to any given slice within the reference polyp (Polyp 3 - b2-42, see Figure S1B and Table S1) in order to account for regions along the polyps that were longer or shorter than in the reference polyp (Table S1).

By manually inspecting, cluster 1 markers of the intact data were not identiﬁed to be very speciﬁc and, therefore, more cluster-speciﬁc genes were identiﬁed by ﬁnding genes that correlate with the top cluster 1 marker NVEC200-000547.1 (Table S2). Calculating a cell cycle score A cell cycle score was calculated for intact polyps by using Seurat’s AddModuleScore function with default settings after manually intersecting canonical cell cycle markers provided by Seurat with annotated genes in Nematostella by name (see Figures S3A and S3C).

Quantifying differential systemic expression changes between time points We performed two analyses to identify differentially expressed genes between time points. i) The ﬁrst global body-wide differential expression analysis between regeneration time points and the intact state identiﬁed 113 differentially expressed (DE) genes for 12 hpa, 122 for 24 hpa, 110 for 48 hpa and 98 for 96 hpa (Wilcoxon Rank Sum test, log2FC > 1) (Table S3), suggesting a lasting effect of injury on gene expression. In addition, time point speciﬁc DE genes were calculated by using the FindAllMarkers function in Seurat (Wilcoxon Rank Sum test, log2FC > 0.3; Table S3). In both methods we found a huge overlap of genes between adjacent timepoints and decided to pursue another DE analysis strategy. ii) We searched for adjacent time point markers by applying the FindingMarkers function in Seurat and asking for combined time point speciﬁc markers against all other time points (12/24 hpa: early, 24/48 hpa: medium, 48/96 hpa: late) (Wilcoxon Rank Sum test, log2FC > 0.25 & < -0.25; Table S3). Top 50 positive markers for each of the three DE analyses were used as input for a GO term enrichment analysis using the R package ‘GOseq’34 (Table S3). The p value cutoff for signiﬁcant GO terms was 0.05 and the enriched terms belonging to the category ‘biological process’ (BP) were visualized using ‘Revigo’60 by automatically lumping similar terms.

Quantifying differential local expression changes between time points Log-normalized counts for gene expression for polyps in the common coordinate space obtained by dynamic time warping were used in a GPCounts model38 to ﬁt Gaussian processes. Brieﬂy, when comparing two-time points, three models are considered: one per time point and one joint model. The log-likelihood of the joint model is then compared to the log-likelihoods of individual models, and a chi-squared test is used to determine the signiﬁcance of the difference. Signiﬁcant genes (FDR<1%) are chosen as spatially differentially expressed (DE) between these time points. For each of the spatially DE genes at each time point, the distance between the mean values of the ﬁt and the baseline (the mean of the ﬁt in intact samples) was then calculated as follows:

dðgi; tp1; gi; tp2Þ

where i refers to equally spaced numbers in the (0, 1) interval along the animal (normalized position value), tp1 and tp2 denote two time points and d is a distance metric (Euclidean distance). GO term enrichment analysis was performed using the R package ‘GOseq’34 with all 702 DE genes that vary in space and time as identiﬁed by Gaussian ﬁtting being used as input. The p-value cutoff applied was 0.02.

These images were analysed using FIJI. For each polyp, the straight line tool was used to measure the body length from the mouth to the aboral end, and the segmented line tool was used to measure the polyp area, excluding the tentacles. The average width of each polyp was computed by dividing the area by the length. To approximate the shape, the aspect ratio of each polyp was deﬁned as the length divided by the average width. Quantiﬁcation of Col4::dendra2 dynamics Dendra2, a photoconvertible protein that transforms from green (488 nm) to red (561 nm) upon excitation with UV (405nm), was endogenously tagged to Col 4. Polyps (3 weeks old) maintained at 23C expressing Col4::Dendra2 were anesthetized with 7% MgCl2 in 12 ppt ASW and mounted on 35 mm dishes (MatTek, P35G-1.5-14-C). Col4::Dendra2 was photoconverted at 4 different regions along the oral-aboral axis using a Zeiss LSM880 Airy confocal microscope. Following that, the animals were washed and returned to 12 ppt ASW. The physa amputation was done by slicing off tissue below the mesenteries with a sharp knife. The polyps were anesthetized 18 hours post amputation (HPA) and imaged with the same microscope. To understand the dynamics of Col4, the positions of the photo-converted clones (xk) were recorded for the control and regenerating polyps after photoconversion (t = t0) and 18 hours post amputation (HPA) (t = t1). The length of every polyp was normalized from the mouth opening (x = 0) to aboral end (x = 1) with the length of the animals at t0. The positions were determined on resliced images from the Z-stack to calculate the exact distance from the mouth. This allows quantifying a relative velocity ﬁeld for Col4::Dendra2 by computing v(xk,t) = xk(t0) - xk(t1), where k denotes the position of the clone along the axis. The plot approximates a ﬁeld of Col4 remodeling during regeneration, with the x-axis representing axial position and y-axis representing the velocity of Col4::Dendra2 towards oral (positive) or aboral pole (negative). The shaded area represents a 95% conﬁdence interval with the ﬁtting of a linear model.

After removing the substrate solution, two washing steps were performed in the dark with 12 ppt ASW for 5 min. Then, the animals were anesthetized with 7% MgCl2 and ﬁxed for 30 min with ice-cold 4% paraformaldehyde/PBS at room temperature and washed 2x 5 min with PBS. The polyps were kept for at least o/n at 4C in a Vectashield mounting medium with DAPI (Vector Laboratories) before being mounted and imaged on a Leica SP8 confocal system. The measurements were obtained from resliced images of the Z-stack to accurately calculate the distance from the mouth. Following spawning, Fgfrb-EGFP embryos were grown at 23C.
